message.content:
### Tenant Rights in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | Key Rights | How to Exercise Them | |------|------------|----------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after the lease ends, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, livable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, etc.).
• Must comply with all local building and health codes. | • Document problems with photos and written notices.
• If the landlord fails to fix issues, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek a court order. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on how much rent can be increased, but it must be in writing and given **at least 30 days’ notice** for month‑to‑month tenants and **60 days’ notice** for fixed‑term leases. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses.
• If you’re a month‑to‑month tenant, you can refuse to pay a rent increase that isn’t properly notified. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: Landlord must give **30 days’ notice** before the lease expires if they intend not to renew. | • Keep written notices and confirm receipt with the other party. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter the premises without **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) unless it’s an emergency. | • If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint or seek damages. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but only if you follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time to fix, etc.). | • Keep receipts and document the issue. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must provide a **written notice** (usually 3 days for nonpayment, 30 days for lease violations).
• Eviction must go through the court; landlords cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond to notices promptly; consider legal counsel if facing eviction. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord must respect your privacy; they can’t conduct searches without a warrant or a court order. | • Report any unlawful entry or search to the police or a lawyer. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide a written statement of utility responsibilities. | • Verify who pays for utilities and keep records. | | **Subletting** | • You may sublet only if the lease allows it or with the landlord’s written consent. | • Get written permission and keep a copy. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas has free legal aid for low‑income tenants (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center). | • Contact local legal aid or tenant advocacy groups. | #### Quick Tips 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – It’s the primary document governing your rights and responsibilities. 2. **Keep Records** – Photos, emails, text messages, and written notices are your best evidence. 3. **Know the Timeline** – Notice periods and deadlines are strict; missing them can cost you. 4. **Seek Help Early** – If you’re unsure about a landlord’s action, consult a lawyer or tenant advocacy group before it escalates. Feel free to ask if you need more detail on any specific area!
